record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: In fully decentralized or peer-to-peer federated learning, where no central server orchestrates training and clients communicate over a possibly dynamic graph, what governance or trust mechanism should decide the model, algorithm, hyperparameters, and debugging responsibility for a learning task?

evidence.quote: Who decides what is the model to be trained in the decentralized setting?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider a fully decentralized (peer-to-peer) federated learning system consisting of a set of clients $\{1,\dots,N\}$, each holding a local dataset $\mathcal{D}_i$, communicating over a (possibly time-varying) connected graph $G_t = (V, E_t)$ with no central coordinator. The clients wish to collaboratively train a model by exchanging messages only along edges of $G_t$. A "learning task specification" consists of: (i) the model class (architecture, parameter space), (ii) the training algorithm (e.g., decentralized SGD, gossip averaging, etc.), (iii) the hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, communication schedule, stopping criterion), and (iv) the assignment of responsibility for monitoring, debugging, and correcting failures during training. Design a formal governance / trust mechanism — i.e., a distributed protocol $\Pi$ executed on $G_t$, together with a decision rule $\mathcal{R}$ — such that the clients can collectively agree upon and update the learning task specification in a way that satisfies the following desiderata: (a) correctness: the agreed-upon specification is well-defined and consistent across all honest clients; (b) incentive compatibility: no client (or coalition of size below a specified threshold) can unilaterally impose a specification that benefits itself at the expense of others; (c) robustness: the mechanism tolerates a bounded fraction of Byzantine or unresponsive clients and adapts to changes in $G_t$; (d) accountability: every decision can be traced to an identifiable subset of clients who can be held responsible for debugging. Either exhibit such a mechanism $(\Pi, \mathcal{R})$ together with a proof of properties (a)–(d), or prove that no protocol satisfying (a)–(d) simultaneously can exist under stated assumptions on the communication and adversary models.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of governance and trust mechanisms in fully decentralized federated learning remains an active open research direction. Recent surveys and works on decentralized/peer-to-peer FL (often combining gossip protocols with blockchain or DAG-based consensus) propose partial solutions but no widely accepted formal mechanism simultaneously providing correctness, incentive compatibility, Byzantine robustness, and accountability has been established.

status_evidence.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Lists governance and decision-making in fully decentralized FL as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The original compendium explicitly poses governance in decentralized FL as unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Decentralized Federated Learning: A Survey and Perspective
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys decentralized FL approaches including blockchain-based trust, gossip learning, and identifies open governance and incentive challenges.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent surveys continue to list governance/trust as open.
